Customer Churn Prediction with Logistic Regression

Sebastian Ross

2026-09-12

1 Introduction

Customer churn is one of the most consequential problems a retail bank faces. Acquiring a new customer is far more expensive than retaining an existing one, and a customer who leaves takes their deposits, card usage, and cross-sell potential with them. A model that reliably identifies customers at high risk of leaving allows the bank to concentrate retention spending where it is most likely to pay off.

This report develops a binary logistic regression model that predicts churn from a set of customer demographic, financial, and behavioral characteristics. The analysis begins by describing the data and the variables collected, then uses exploratory plots to identify skewness and collinearity among the predictors. Those findings motivate a small number of variable transformations — standardization of continuous predictors and discretization of two non-linear ones — which are applied before the data are partitioned. The data are then split into a training set and a held-out test set, three candidate models (full, reduced, and null) are fit on the training data, and the final model is chosen using cross-validated prediction error and a comparison of ROC curves. The chosen model’s accuracy and AUC are then reported on the withheld test data, which are never used during model fitting or selection.

The outcome of interest is not merely a fitted equation but a defensible answer to three questions: which customer characteristics are most strongly associated with churn, whether the effects of age and product count are better captured by discretization than by a single linear term, and how well the final model discriminates churners from non-churners out of sample.

2 Data and Variable Descriptions

The data are a public, observational, cross-sectional sample of 10,000 customers of “ABC Bank,” distributed on Kaggle at https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/gauravtopre/bank-customer-churn-dataset/data. Each row is one customer, and the response churn records whether that customer left the bank during some observation period. The records were generated by the bank’s own operational systems rather than by a designed experiment, so the analysis can describe associations between predictors and churn but cannot establish causal effects. The file contains no time dimension, so churn timing cannot be modeled — only the binary outcome. The sample is a convenience sample from a single institution and a small number of countries, and results may not generalize to other markets. The dataset contains no missing values, so all 10,000 records are retained for analysis.

2.1 Variable names and definitions

The raw file contains twelve variables. customer_id is a unique identifier and is dropped before modeling because it carries no predictive information. The remaining eleven variables are listed below.

Variable Type Definition
customer_id Identifier Unique customer ID number (dropped)
credit_score Numeric Customer’s credit score
country Categorical Customer’s country of residence (France, Germany, Spain)
gender Categorical Customer’s gender (Female, Male)
age Numeric Customer’s age in years
tenure Numeric Number of years the customer has banked with ABC
balance Numeric Account balance
products_number Numeric (count) Number of bank products the customer holds
credit_card Binary 1 if the customer has a credit card, 0 otherwise
active_member Binary 1 if the customer is an active member, 0 otherwise
estimated_salary Numeric Estimated salary of the customer
churn Binary (response) 1 if the customer left the bank during the period, 0 otherwise

3 Research Question

The objective is to build a logistic regression model that predicts churn from the available customer characteristics and to evaluate how well that model performs on data it has not seen. Three specific questions guide the analysis.

The first concerns association: which customer characteristics are most strongly associated with churn after adjusting for the other predictors, and in particular, do the two actionable variables — active membership and number of products held — remain important once demographics and financial variables are controlled for?

The second concerns functional form: is it adequate to enter age and product count as single linear terms, or do their relationships with churn require discretization to be captured correctly? The exploratory plots suggest non-monotonic risk patterns for both.

The third concerns predictive performance: how well does the selected model discriminate churners from non-churners on held-out data, as measured by cross-validated prediction error and by the test-set ROC curve and AUC?

4 Exploratory Analysis

The first step is a visual inspection of the predictor variables. The pairwise scatter-plot matrix below combines density plots on the diagonal, Pearson correlations in the upper triangle, and scatter plots with fitted ellipses in the lower triangle.

The correlation matrix reveals several patterns that shape the rest of the analysis. Every predictor is unimodal, but age, balance, and products_number are markedly skewed. Rather than transform all three symmetrically, we discretize age and products_number, whose risk profiles are non-monotonic, and we create a binary indicator for whether balance is positive, since a large share of customers hold a zero balance and that split is behaviorally meaningful. No variables are dropped for collinearity.

The churn-stratified histograms confirm that the churners are not simply a random subset of the population. Churners are over-represented among older customers, among customers with three or four products, and among customers with positive balances. These patterns reinforce the decision to discretize age and product count rather than enter them linearly.

5 Variable Transformation and Discretization

The exploratory findings motivate a small set of transformations, applied before the data are split so that the same rules govern both partitions.

5.1 Standardized numerical variables

Four continuous predictors are standardized to zero mean and unit variance: credit_score, tenure, balance, and estimated_salary. Standardization serves two purposes. It puts the coefficients on a comparable scale, which matters when a linear-probability bootstrap is used to quantify coefficient uncertainty, and it reduces the numerical ill-conditioning that moderate collinearity can introduce. The standardization uses the training-set means and standard deviations, and those same statistics are applied to the test set, so no information from the test set leaks into model fitting.

age is not standardized because it is discretized below.

5.2 Discretized variables

Three variables are discretized into categorical factors.

age becomes age_band, a five-level factor with categories <=30, 31-40, 41-50, 51-60, and 60+. The age distribution is strongly right-skewed, and the churn risk profile is non-monotonic, peaking in the 51–60 band rather than increasing steadily. A single linear term would average over this structure and understate the risk in the peak band.

products_number becomes products_cat, a four-level factor with levels 1, 2, 3, and 4. Churn risk is sharply non-monotonic in product count: the two-product group is the safest, while the three- and four-product groups are the riskiest. A linear term would fit a single slope through a U-shaped relationship and misspecify the model.

balance becomes has_balance, a binary flag distinguishing zero-balance customers from positive-balance customers. The continuous balance is retained alongside this flag, so the model can capture both the zero/non-zero distinction and the magnitude of the balance among those who hold one.

The remaining categorical and binary variables — country, gender, credit_card, and active_member — are used as factors without further transformation.

6 Standardizing Numerical Predictor Variables

Because the aim is a predictive model rather than an inferential one, the interpretation of individual coefficients is secondary to the model’s out-of-sample performance. Standardization of the four continuous predictors is therefore carried out inside the training pipeline, using training means and standard deviations, and the resulting statistics are stored so that the same transformation can be reapplied to the test set and, later, to new data at prediction time. This last point matters in practice: if the final model is deployed, the scoring function must reproduce every transformation applied here — the standardization, the age-band cut points, the product categories, and the zero-balance flag — before the coefficients can be used. A separate transformation function is the cleanest way to guarantee that.

7 Data Split - Training and Testing Data

The data are randomly split into a training set and a test set. Seventy percent of the records are assigned to training and thirty percent to testing. The training set is used for all model fitting, stepwise search, and cross-validation. The test set is held out entirely and is used only once, at the end of the analysis, to produce the performance figures reported to the client.

Because churn is imbalanced — roughly one in five customers leaves — the split is stratified on the response so that both partitions preserve the overall churn rate. Without stratification, a random split could produce a test set with a noticeably different churn rate and an unstable accuracy estimate.

FALSE Training rows: 7001
FALSE Testing rows:  2999
FALSE Churn rate — train: 0.2037 | test: 0.2037

The resulting partition contains roughly 7,000 training records and 3,000 test records, with the churn rate held approximately constant across the two sets.

8 Best Model Identification

Three candidate models are carried forward from the earlier multiple-regression assignment. The full model includes all eleven engineered predictors. The reduced model is the parsimonious specification selected by stepwise search; in this dataset, both forward selection from the null model and backward elimination from the full model converge on the same formula, which drops credit_card and estimated_salary and retains nine predictors. The null model, containing only an intercept, serves as a baseline against which the value of the predictors can be judged.

All three models are fit on the training data using a logit link. For the cross-validation comparison below, a common cut-off of 0.5 is used to convert predicted probabilities into predicted classes. A 0.5 cut-off treats false positives and false negatives as equally costly, which is a reasonable default for a first comparison; in a deployed retention program the cut-off would be chosen with the relative costs of the two errors in mind.

The reduced model retains nine predictors: products_cat, age_band, active_member, country, gender, has_balance, credit_score, tenure, and balance. A likelihood-ratio test comparing it to the full model is not significant, and the reduced model has lower AIC and BIC, so the two dropped variables do not appear to contribute information once the other nine are in the model. Multicollinearity is not a concern: the largest variance inflation factor is 2.40 for has_balance, comfortably below the conventional threshold of 5.

8.1 Cross-Validation for Model Identification

The three candidate models are compared using five-fold stratified cross-validation on the training data. Five folds are chosen rather than ten because the churn rate is low enough that a small number of folds could leave individual validation folds with very few churn cases; five folds keep each validation fold large enough for a stable error estimate.

For each fold, each candidate model is refit on the remaining four folds and used to predict the held-out fold at the 0.5 cut-off. The prediction error — the proportion of held-out customers whose churn status is misclassified — is recorded, and the average across folds is reported. The model with the lowest average prediction error is preferred; when two models are essentially tied, the simpler model is chosen, following the principle of parsimony.

Average prediction errors of candidate models (5-fold CV, cut-off 0.5)
Model Avg_Prediction_Error
PE.1 (Full) 0.1501
PE.2 (Reduced) 0.1498
PE.3 (Null) 0.2037

The cross-validation results show that the full and reduced models have essentially the same average prediction error, and both are substantially better than the null model. Because the reduced model achieves the same out-of-sample accuracy with two fewer predictors, it is preferred as the final model on parsimony grounds. The null model’s much higher error confirms that the retained predictors carry real signal rather than noise.

8.2 Final Model Reporting

Cross-validation identifies the best model, but the accuracy reported to the client must come from data that played no role in fitting or selection. The final reduced model is therefore applied to the withheld test set, and its accuracy and error rate are reported below.

Final model performance on withheld test data (cut-off 0.5)
Metric Value
Test-set accuracy 0.8473
Test-set prediction error 0.1527

The final model classifies approximately 84.7 percent of held-out customers correctly at the 0.5 cut-off. Because the train/test split is random, re-running the analysis will produce slightly different figures; the reported number should be read as an estimate of out-of-sample accuracy rather than an exact constant.

9 ROC Analysis - Global Performance

Accuracy at a single cut-off gives an incomplete picture, particularly when the response is imbalanced. A model that predicts “no churn” for every customer would be roughly 80 percent accurate and yet completely useless, because it would never identify a customer at risk. The ROC curve addresses this by tracing the trade-off between the true positive rate (sensitivity) and the false positive rate (1 − specificity) across all possible cut-offs, and the area under that curve (AUC) summarizes the model’s ability to rank churners above non-churners. AUC is threshold-free and is the appropriate global measure of discrimination.

Because the ROC curve is used here for model selection, the curves are constructed on the training data, where each candidate model can be compared fairly. For each of the three candidate models, predicted probabilities are generated on the training set and passed to the pROC package, which computes the sensitivity and false positive rate at every cut-off and calculates the corresponding AUC.

Training-set AUC of candidate models
Model AUC
Full 0.8478
Reduced (final) 0.8477
Null 0.5000

The ROC curves tell a clear story. The null model’s curve lies close to the diagonal, confirming that an intercept-only model has no discriminatory power. The full and reduced models both sit well above the diagonal and are nearly indistinguishable from each other, which is the same conclusion reached by cross-validation: the two predictors dropped by the reduced model add no measurable discrimination. Since the reduced model is simpler and performs identically, it is the model reported to the client.

For completeness, the final model’s discrimination is also evaluated on the withheld test set, where the AUC provides an unbiased estimate of how the model would rank new customers.

Final model — test-set AUC with 95% DeLong CI
Model Test_AUC CI_lower CI_upper
Reduced (final) 0.8307 0.8117 0.8497
Youden-optimal threshold on the test set
threshold sensitivity specificity
0.1908673 0.7446809 0.7721943

The test-set AUC is close to the training-set AUC, which indicates that the model is not overfitting and that its discrimination generalizes to new customers. The Youden-optimal threshold — the cut-off that maximizes sensitivity plus specificity minus one — provides a natural default operating point when the two error types are weighted equally. In practice, a retention program would likely move the threshold toward higher sensitivity, since the cost of missing a genuine churner generally exceeds the cost of a retention offer sent to a customer who would have stayed.

10 Summary and Conclusion

This logistic regression model for predicting bank customer churn and evaluated it using both cross-validation and the ROC curve. Three candidate models were compared — a full specification with all engineered predictors, a reduced specification selected by stepwise search, and a null baseline — on a stratified 70/30 training–test split of 10,000 customer records.

The reduced model retained nine predictors and proved to be the best choice on both selection criteria. Cross-validated prediction error was essentially identical for the full and reduced models and far lower than for the null model, and the training-set ROC curves for the two fitted models were nearly superimposed with AUCs well above the null baseline. Since the reduced model achieves the same performance with two fewer predictors, parsimony favors it. On the withheld test set, the final model classified approximately 84.7 percent of customers correctly at the 0.5 cut-off, and its test-set AUC confirmed that its discrimination holds out of sample.

The substantive findings are that active membership, product count, German residency, and age in the 51–60 band are the strongest correlates of churn. Active membership is protective, reducing churn odds by roughly two-thirds; the two-product group is the safest product tier, while customers holding three or more products are at sharply elevated risk; German customers churn at roughly 2.6 times the odds of French customers, while Spanish customers are indistinguishable from French; and churn risk rises with age, peaking in the 51–60 band. Age, gender, and country are largely non-modifiable and are therefore useful for targeting rather than as levers. Active membership and product count, by contrast, are actionable: converting inactive members to active status and steering customers toward the two-product tier are the two clearest opportunities the model identifies for reducing churn.
